Academic Foundation

Trained to read the water column before advising on the carbon market above it.

Her consulting work is built on a formal oceanography background — physical water-mass analysis in Indonesian waters — the same quantitative, evidence-first habits she now applies to climate-adaptation and carbon-market advisory. This grounding is directly relevant to research priorities in environmental governance and natural-resource management, such as those pursued at Wageningen University & Research: linking biophysical data to policy-relevant, real-world decision-making.

Physical Oceanography Research — Characterised water-mass structure and mixing in Indonesian shelf and open-ocean waters using CTD/model salinity–temperature data, producing potential-temperature/salinity (θ-S) water-mass diagrams and validating model output against field measurements (R² = 0.886 salinity correlation).

This research trained the same skills now applied commercially: turning raw environmental data into a defensible, evidence-based case — the backbone of due-diligence work for Nature-based Solutions (NbS) and carbon-project screening.

"From θ-S diagrams to due-diligence matrices — the method is the same: let the data draw the boundary."

Why it matters

The same discipline — sourcing reliable data, testing it against a model, and only then drawing conclusions — now shapes how she screens corporate partners and NbS projects for climate-finance incubation.

Carbon Offsets & Carbon Pricing

Testing whether a credit holds up before it is priced.

Most project work sits under Verra VCS, Gold Standard and Plan Vivo. Technical checks come first; pricing and policy analysis follow, so that a credit's price reflects its quality and the rules it will be sold under.

Offset development

Field & restoration stages
Data & MRV stages
Market outcome
Peatland lever

Canal blocking & rewetting keep the water table near the surface, halting peat oxidation — the core avoided-emissions mechanism behind most Indonesian peatland carbon projects.

Mangrove lever

Mangrove sediment stores several times more carbon per hectare than terrestrial forest ("blue carbon"), while restored stands rebuild coastal storm and erosion protection.

Case Study · Carbon Project Development

A development strategy for a multi-site forestry carbon pipeline in Indonesia.

Prepared in 2026 for a Hong Kong-based climate-technology consultancy expanding into the Indonesian forestry carbon market. Client and site names are withheld; the pipeline figures are my own work.

Certification roadmap: 0–36 months

A phased path from permit due diligence to first credit issuance, following the Verra VCS and CCB pathway with a third-party validator.

Phase 0 · 0–3 months

Due diligence & data

  • Confirm forestry-permit (PBPH) validity for each site
  • Audit national registry status
  • Map local communities and customary (adat) rights
  • Regulatory scan against PP 23/2021 (forestry)
Phase 1 · 3–9 months

Pre-assessment & PDD

  • Commission remote sensing (NDVI, deforestation baseline)
  • Select the Verra REDD+ methodology
  • Engage an accredited validator (VVB)
  • Develop the Project Design Document
Phase 2 · 9–18 months

Validation

  • On-site validation visit and community consultation
  • Submit to Verra for registry review
  • Obtain VCS and CCB (co-benefits) certification
  • Register units in Indonesia's carbon unit registry (SRUK)
Phase 3 · 18–36 months

Verification & issuance

  • Monitoring: remote sensing plus field MRV data
  • Annual verification reports to the validator
  • First credit issuance; indicative USD 10–50 per credit depending on standard
  • Offtake via brokers/traders or direct corporate buyers (RE100)

Regulatory landscape: Indonesia carbon market

InstrumentWhat it does
Perpres 110/2025
signed 10 Oct 2025		Replaces Perpres 98/2021 as the framework for carbon economic value (NEK) and national GHG control. Adds carbon allocation and the SRUK unit registry; SRN PPI stays for NDC tracking. A one-year transition applies.
SRUK / SRN PPISRUK records carbon units traded under NEK, including on the carbon exchange; SRN PPI tracks mitigation actions toward the NDC. Projects registered under the older flow need to be mapped across.
Permen LHK 21/2022Ministerial procedures for implementing NEK under the earlier framework (project registration, unit issuance). Status to be checked against the Perpres 110/2025 transition.
PP 23/2021 (forestry)Governs forestry business permits (PBPH) that carry carbon rights; boundary demarcation (penataan batas) must be completed for each concession.
Verra VCS / CCBREDD+ projects need a baseline, monitoring plan, validation by an accredited auditor and registry listing; CCB adds community and biodiversity co-benefits.

Regulatory references updated for Perpres 110/2025 (replacing Perpres 98/2021) and the move from SRN PPI to SRUK for carbon units.

Technical Assessment · Blue Carbon MRV

From registry steps to Mg CO₂e per hectare: a mangrove MRV framework.

A technical answer (original in Bahasa Indonesia) covering end-to-end MRV, planting SOPs, plot design, four-pool carbon measurement and a worked example. It draws on IndoBCR (Murdiyarso et al.), the CIFOR-ICRAF mangrove blue-carbon measurement manual and the 2024 blue-carbon best-practice guide (Simpson & Smart). All example numbers are illustrative.

End-to-end MRV: who does what, and when

#StageActorOutputTiming (IndoBCR)
1Register on SRN PPI; define the work areaProponentRegistry account; boundary (shapefile + metadata)—
2Prepare and submit the DRAM (baseline, monitoring plan)ProponentComplete DRAM with monitoring plan5 working days
3Validate the DRAMIndependent validatorValidated DRAM, recorded in the registry≈ 1 month
4Implement and monitor (plant, plot, measure)Proponent, community groups, field teamPlanting logbook, plot data, monitoring reportMonitor at least every 5 years
5Verify the LCAM (mitigation achievement report)Independent verifierVerification report≈ 6 months
6Decision and issuanceNational registry authorityRegistry code and SPE-GRK14 working days

Selling abroad requires mutual recognition of standards (VCS/Verra, Plan Vivo, ERF). The flow follows IndoBCR, which rests on Perpres 98/2021; the assessment flags that it must be aligned with Perpres 110/2025 and SRUK before implementation.

Four steps that cannot be repeated once missed

IndoBCR §2.1

Boundary and tenure

Every stakeholder must agree the work area before the DRAM. Unavoidable overlaps need a provincial recommendation letter; verifiers check for double claims.

IndoBCR §4

2-year look-back window

Removals can only be claimed up to 2 years before the DRAM is submitted. Delaying registration forfeits older sequestration.

IndoBCR §3

Baseline period

A 5–10 year reference, with no overlap or gap against the claim period; the claim must start within 3 years of the baseline ending.

Method logic

Time-zero and planting-day records

Initial soil and biomass stocks and planting records (date, count, species, location) cannot be reconstructed later. Without t0, ΔC and survival rate cannot be proven.

Plot design: nested circles on a shore-normal transect

Six sub-plots per standard plot, 25 m between centres, the first at 15 m from the seaward-most stand, running landward. Each sub-plot nests a 7 m radius circle for trees (DBH ≥ 5 cm) and a 2 m radius circle for saplings (DBH < 5 cm); seedlings under 1.37 m are counted, and soil and deadwood are sampled in every sub-plot.

Stratified random plot placement in GIS; permanent plots re-measured at the same points
Sample size per stratum: n ≈ (t × CV ÷ E)², from a pre-survey

High-quality standards require reducing uncertainty where the sampling error exceeds 20% (90% CI) or 30% (95% CI). Adding plots lowers error and the uncertainty discount on credits.

Measuring the four carbon pools

PoolWhat is measured, and howEquation and factor
Aboveground biomassTrees (DBH ≥ 5 cm) measured at 1.3 m or above the highest prop root; saplings in the 2 m plot; seedlings counted.Species/site allometry, e.g. A. marina: AGB = 0.1848 × D2.3524 (kg). Carbon = biomass × 0.46.
Belowground biomassCalculated from the same DBH with a root equation.BGB = 1.28 × D1.17 (kg). Carbon = biomass × 0.39.
Deadwood (necromass)Volume of dead wood by size class (van Wagner 1968; Brown 1971).Biomass = volume × specific gravity; carbon = biomass × 0.5.
Soil carbonAuger cores at 5–10, 20–25, 37.5–42.5, 72.5–77.5 and 197.5–202.5 cm; lab dry combustion at 950 °C (bulk density, %C).Soil C (Mg C/ha) = BD (g/cm³) × %C × layer thickness (cm).

Conversion chain: dry biomass (kg) × carbon fraction → kg C ÷ plot area (m²) × 10,000 ÷ 1,000 → Mg C/ha × 3.67 (44/12) → Mg CO₂e/ha. Tree decay-status factors multiply above- and belowground carbon: status 0 = 1, status 1 = 0.975, status 2 = 0.8, status 3 = 0.5.

Worked example: field data to Mg CO₂e/ha

Illustrative data: one 7 m sub-plot (153.94 m²) of A. marina with four trees (DBH 8.5, 12.0, 15.5 and 19.0 cm; tree 4 at decay status 1), and a four-layer soil profile to 100 cm.

2BGB = 1.28 × D1.1715.7 + 23.4 + 31.6 + 40.1110.8 kg
3Tree carbonAGB × 0.46 + BGB × 0.39; tree 4 × 0.975223.4 kg C
4Scale to hectare223.4 kg × 10,000 ÷ 153.94 ÷ 1,00014.51 Mg C/ha
5Soil carbon, 0–100 cm33.6 + 31.2 + 35.7 + 72.0172.5 Mg C/ha
6Total × 3.67(14.51 + 172.5) × 3.67686.3 Mg CO₂e/ha

Mg CO₂e/ha, before project emissions and leakage

Compare ΔC with its standard error, use equivalent soil mass, and deduct project emissions and leakage. Young-seedling indicators: survival = live ÷ planted × 100% per plot and cohort; growth as height and leaf count per semester.

Five principles for defensible carbon numbers

01

Document the baseline

Record initial conditions and boundaries before any action.

02

Measure to the national standard

Standard plots with stratified random sampling.

03

Use national factors

0.46 / 0.39, decay-status factors and 3.67.

04

Trace every number

Back to the individual tree and soil sample.

05

Report uncertainty, not only the mean

Species zoning, planting spacing, re-planting windows, the plot-count formula and funder-report contents come from general restoration practice rather than the reference documents; the survival threshold is an example to be set in the monitoring plan.

Publications & Conferences

Peer-reviewed research, presented internationally.

Published oceanographic research on ENSO dynamics and equatorial water-mass movement, presented at an international conference — and ongoing engagement with Indonesia's climate-finance and carbon-market community as a Nature-based Solutions Analyst.

IOP Conf. Series: Earth & Environmental Science · Open Access

The Dynamic of Convergence Zone Displacement in Western Pacific Ocean on 2015 Super El Niño Event

Ashafahani A A, Wirasatriya A, Pranowo W S, Sugianto D N, Maslukah L (2021). IOP Conf. Ser.: Earth Environ. Sci. 750 012015. doi:10.1088/1755-1315/750/1/012015

Presented at the 6th International Conference on Tropical and Coastal Region Eco-Development. Used satellite SST/SSS, Argo float and Copernicus reanalysis data to track the Pacific warm-pool convergence zone (isotherm 28.5°C / isohaline 34.6 psu) through the 2015 Super El Niño, and linked its displacement to skipjack tuna catch patterns.

  • Convergence zone shifted as far east as 136°W during the Super El Niño — vs. 154°E during La Niña.
  • North Equatorial Counter Current strengthened by 0.8 m/s, the key driver pushing the warm pool eastward.
  • Strong positive correlation (R = 0.82–0.88) between SST and skipjack tuna CPUE across ENSO phases.

Coastal Community Action

"Facing the Sea 2.0" — coastal clean-up & marine-litter research, Maroon Beach, Semarang.

As Executive of Research & Development, Youth Maritime of Central Java, led community coastal clean-up and public-education work on marine litter and microplastics at Maroon Beach — connecting hands-on fieldwork with the same coastal-resilience themes that now inform her climate-adaptation advisory.

Field finding

A plastic bottle takes at least 450 years to degrade — up to 1,000 years for PET/PETE — and 90% are never recycled. Marine debris is increasing by roughly 5%/year despite growing clean-up effort.

Regional context

Sampling across Indonesia found 55% of fish species examined contained human-derived debris — 28% of individual fish sampled, with one specimen carrying 21 separate plastic pieces.
